pl-l3d3c4-d1e117.summary: Concludes that Christ is rightly said to have assumed the first fruits of our mass, since he took not the flesh of sin but the likeness of sinful flesh.
claims: Christ assumed the likeness of sinful flesh, not sinful flesh.

pl-l3d3c4-d1e120.summary: Expounds Rom 8:3: the Word assumed flesh like sinful flesh in penalty, not guilt; all other human flesh is of sin, but not his, since his mother conceived him by grace, not concupiscence. He has the likeness of sinful flesh through passibility and mortality, hunger and thirst. His flesh is the same as ours, but was not made the same way: it was sanctified in the womb and born without sin, and he never sinned. It lacked the pollution conceived from concupiscence and the vice that causes sin in others, so it was not bound to sin.
claims: Christ's flesh was like ours in penalty but not guilt.
Christ's flesh was conceived by grace, not concupiscence.
Christ's flesh was not bound to sin.

pl-l3d3c4-d1e129.summary: Raises an apparent objection to the view that the Word's flesh was not conceived before being assumed: Augustine on John 2:19–20 ('forty-six years was this temple built') says the number fits the perfection of the Lord's body, since physicians say the form of the human body is completed in that many days.

pl-l3d3c4-d1e145.summary: Reports that some, from Augustine's words, presumed to say that the Lord's body was formed and distinguished into members over those days like other bodies, and only then did the Word unite flesh and soul to himself.
claims: Some held that the Word was united to the body only after it was formed.

pl-l3d3c4-d1e148.summary: Gives the correct reading: Augustine did not deny that as soon as the flesh was sanctified and separated by the Spirit it was united with the soul to the Word, making him perfect God and perfect man; rather, the distinction of the members at the moment of conception and union was so slight as to be barely visible, and became perfect and noticeable over those days.
claims: The Word was united to flesh and soul at the moment of conception.
Christ's members became visibly distinct over the following days.

pl-l3d3c4-d1e154.summary: Closes with John Damascene: the Word was incarnate without leaving his incorporeality; he was wholly incarnate and wholly uncircumscribed, made small and contracted bodily but uncircumscribed divinely, his flesh not coextensive with his divinity. He was in all things and above all, and in the womb of his mother in the very act of incarnation.
claims: The incarnate Word remained uncircumscribed in his divinity.

pl-l3d3c4.summary: Concludes that Christ assumed the first fruits of our mass: not the flesh of sin but the likeness of sinful flesh (Rom 8:3), like ours in penalty (passibility, mortality, hunger, thirst) but not guilt, conceived by grace not concupiscence. It addresses an apparent conflict with simultaneous conception: Augustine's remark that 46 days perfect the human body's form, which some take to mean the body was formed before union. Lombard explains that union was immediate, but the members were too tiny to see at first and became distinct in those days. With Damascene, the Word was incarnate without leaving his incorporeality, wholly in the womb yet uncircumscribed.
claims: Christ assumed the likeness of sinful flesh, not sinful flesh.
Christ's flesh shared our penalty but not our guilt.
The Word was united to soul and flesh at the moment of conception.
The incarnate Word remained uncircumscribed in his divinity.
